newsitem.title: USA: Study shows wide range of car airbag safety.
newsitem.headline: Study shows wide range of car airbag safety.

text.p: Automobile airbags that deploy vertically up the windscreen are safer than airbags that pop out horizontally toward the passenger, consumer advocates said on Thursday.

Forty-three deaths in low-speed crashes have been linked to airbags that inflated directly into the passenger's chest or face, while none have been linked to vertically inflating airbags used on several models by Honda and Nissan and the 1996-97 Ford Taurus, according to a study by Public Citizen and the Centre for Auto Safety.

"This study shows some airbags are much better than others. Consumers will want to know which type they have in their cars before deciding whether to turn them off," Joan Claybook, president of Public Citizen, told a news conference.

But an organisation that represents auto insurance companies said the study was misleading. "Claiming that deployment direction alone makes the difference between a 'safe' and a 'dangerous' airbag betrays a lack of knowledge about the sophistication of airbag design engineering in today's vehicles," Brian O'Neill, president of the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, said in a statement.
Any child on top of or very close to an airbag when it starts to deploy is at risk, regardless of the deployment direction, O'Neill said.

The consumer advocates' study said deaths occured in vehicles with front-deploying airbags that had "an inadequate safety zone" for the passenger. It said those included Chrysler's Dodge Caravan, Ford's Aspire, Contour, Escort and Mustang and General Motors' Geo Metro.

Because of deaths linked to airbags that may slam into passengers, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is evaluating whether to allow consumers to deactivate passenger airbags. The consumer advocates said they opposed a broad government authorisation to deactivate airbags, saying that would increase risks for most consumers.

But they said the government must do more to inform consumers of differences in airbags including issues such as rates of inflation, sensor performance, the minimum vehicle speed upon impact that will trigger inflation of the airbag, and the type of deployment of the bag.

"Our study suggests that some designs reduce fatalities but the government needs to tell the public exactly which cars have the safest airbags," Clarence Ditlow, executive director of the Centre for Auto Safety, said.

Car buyers also should ask the dealer or the manufacturer whether the passenger airbag inflates vertically or horizontally and factor that into a car-buying decision, Claybrook said. Not all airbags mounted on top of the dash board deploy vertically but virtually all that are mounted on the front of the dash deploy horizontally, she said.

In addition to pushing vertically deploying airbags, the consumer groups said manufacturers should use available technology to raise the deployment threshold on the passenger airbag to 15 miles (24 km) per hour rather than matching the eight or nine mph threshold needed to protect the driver from hitting the steering column.

They also said manufacturers should use better sensors that do not trigger below the threshold speed or late in the crash, deep-dish steering wheels to move the airbag away from the driver and airbag compartmentalization and fold patterns to avoid injury to passengers who are out of position.
